title: Plant Kingdom
tagline: Algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms: the plant line and its alternation of generations.

overview.intro: The plant kingdom is a story of progressive adaptation to land, told through five great groups that differ in how they transport water, how they reproduce and how much of their life cycle is dependent on water. This chapter works through the thalloid algae and their three classes, the bryophytes as the amphibians of the plant kingdom, the pteridophytes as the first vascular plants, and then the seed plants — gymnosperms with naked seeds and angiosperms with flowers and double fertilisation — before bringing the whole sequence together under the idea of alternation of generations. The examiner’s three standing questions are a classification of an unknown plant into one of these groups, a comparison table between two groups, and a life-cycle question on alternation of generations.

facts.label: Five groups
facts.value: Thallophyta or algae, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnospermae and Angiospermae, in increasing complexity of body and vascularity.

facts.label: Alternation of generations
facts.value: A diploid sporophyte produces spores by meiosis, and a haploid gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis; the two phases alternate in the life cycle.

facts.label: Algal pigments
facts.value: Chlorophyll a and b in green algae, a and c with fucoxanthin in brown algae, and a and d with phycoerythrin in red algae.

facts.label: Double fertilisation
facts.value: Unique to angiosperms: one sperm fuses with the egg and a second with the two polar nuclei, giving embryo and endosperm.

learningOutcomes: Classify the plant kingdom into the five groups and state the defining feature of each.
Compare the three classes of algae on pigments, stored food and cell wall composition.
Describe the life cycles of a liverwort, a fern and a flowering plant with the alternation of generations.
Distinguish gymnosperms from angiosperms and give the significance of the seed and the flower.
Identify an unknown plant from a description and justify its placement with diagnostic characters.

blocks.text: Algae are the simplest plants: thalloid bodies that are not differentiated into root, stem and leaf, largely aquatic, and ranging from single cells to large seaweeds. Their body, the thallus, has no vascular tissue and no true embryo, and attachment to a substrate is by a holdfast that anchors but does not absorb as a root does. The group is divided into three classes by pigment, stored food and wall composition. Chlorophyceae, the green algae, contain chlorophyll a and b with carotenoids in chloroplasts that may hold a single pyrenoid; they store food as starch and have walls of cellulose, and examples include Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra with its spiral chloroplasts, Ulva the sea lettuce and the colonial Volvox. Phaeophyceae, the brown algae, are mainly marine and seaweeds such as Fucus, Laminaria and Sargassum; they contain chlorophyll a and c with the brown pigment fucoxanthin, store food as laminarin and mannitol, and have walls of algin and cellulose, with a body built of a holdfast, a stipe and a blade-like frond, and a life cycle with an isomorphic alternation of generations. Rhodophyceae, the red algae, contain chlorophyll a and d with the red pigment phycoerythrin, which allows them to photosynthesise at depth because red light penetrates deepest; they store food as floridean starch, include Polysiphonia, Gelidium from which agar is obtained and Gracilaria, and their sexual reproduction involves a distinctive non-motile spermatangium with no flagellated male gametes at all.

items: Algae: thalloid, no root, stem or leaf, no vascular tissue, mostly aquatic and attached by a holdfast.
Chlorophyceae: chlorophyll a and b, starch stored, cellulose wall; Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra, Ulva, Volvox.
Phaeophyceae: chlorophyll a and c with fucoxanthin, laminarin and mannitol stored, algin in the wall; Fucus, Laminaria, Sargassum.
Rhodophyceae: chlorophyll a and d with phycoerythrin, floridean starch stored; Polysiphonia, Gelidium for agar, Gracilaria.
The brown and red algae have an isomorphic alternation of generations, with the two phases alike in form.
Agar and algin are commercially obtained from red and brown algae respectively.

items.note: A green filament sliding through the hands shows the spiral chloroplasts under the microscope, which give the genus its name and make identification immediate.
Agar used to solidify culture plates is extracted from Gelidium and Gracilaria, which is why the red algae have an economic importance far beyond their size.

items.meaning: A plant body not differentiated into true root, stem and leaf.
The anchoring structure of an alga, which grips the substrate without absorbing like a root.
The brown pigment of Phaeophyceae that masks the green of chlorophyll.
A life cycle in which the sporophyte and gametophyte generations look alike.

blocks.text: Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant kingdom: they live on damp land but their sperm are flagellated and must swim through a film of water to reach the egg, so reproduction still ties them to moisture. The group includes the liverworts such as Riccia and Marchantia with a flat thalloid or leafy body and gemmae cups for asexual reproduction, the mosses such as Funaria and Sphagnum with a leafy gametophyte bearing rhizoids, and the hornworts. The dominant generation is the gametophyte, the green photosynthetic plant that we recognise, while the sporophyte is a small dependent structure of seta and capsule that remains attached to and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte. Pteridophytes take the decisive step: they are the first plants with true vascular tissue, xylem and phloem, so water and dissolved minerals can be conducted through the body and the plant can grow upright and large. Their body is differentiated into true root, stem and leaf, examples include the ferns such as Dryopteris and Pteris and the horsetail Equisetum, and the dominant generation reverses to the sporophyte, which is the conspicuous leafy fern, while the gametophyte is a small heart-shaped prothallus that lives independently on damp soil. Reproduction still needs water because the antherozoids swim to the archegonium, which is why ferns are found in moist shaded habitats. In both groups the spores are produced in sporangia, in ferns typically gathered into sori on the underside of the fronds.

items: Bryophytes: no vascular tissue, rhizoids for anchorage, dominant gametophyte, sporophyte attached and dependent.
Liverworts such as Riccia and Marchantia reproduce asexually by gemmae formed in gemmae cups.
Mosses such as Funaria and Sphagnum have a leafy gametophyte and a capsule borne on a seta.
Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because water is needed for fertilisation.
Pteridophytes: the first vascular plants, with true roots, stems and leaves and dominant sporophyte generation.
Fern spores are borne in sori on the undersides of fronds, and the prothallus is a small independent gametophyte.
Both groups have flagellated sperm and therefore depend on moisture for sexual reproduction.

blocks.caption: Bryophytes against pteridophytes
rows: no, only rhizoids and leaf-like structures
moist but able to grow larger and upright

items.note: The flat green thallus bears cup-shaped gemmae that are splashed out by raindrops and grow into new plants, a common examination specimen for asexual reproduction.
The tall leafy fern is the sporophyte, and beneath each frond the sori release spores that grow into a heart-shaped prothallus no larger than a fingernail.

blocks.text: Seed plants solved the problem that stopped the ferns: instead of flagellated sperm swimming to an egg, pollen carries the male gamete to the ovule through a pollen tube, so fertilisation no longer needs free water. Gymnosperms bear their seeds naked on the scales of a cone rather than enclosed in a fruit, and the group includes conifers such as Pinus and Cedrus, the cycad Cycas with its palm-like appearance and motile sperm, and Ginkgo, the only living species of its lineage. Conifers are adapted to cold and dry conditions with needle-like leaves bearing a thick cuticle and sunken stomata, resin canals, and seeds with winged coats that the wind disperses. Angiosperms, the flowering plants, are the dominant land plants: the seed is enclosed within a fruit developed from the ovary, the flowers are specialised reproductive structures with calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, and they show double fertilisation in which one sperm fuses with the egg to form the embryo and a second fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm, so nutritive tissue is produced only if fertilisation succeeds. The two groups also differ in vessel elements, which angiosperm xylem possesses and most gymnosperm xylem lacks, in broad leaves and in far more efficient reproduction. Between them the two seed-bearing groups show the evolutionary trade-off that the examination expects you to state: the gymnosperm strategy of wind-pollinated cones in harsh climates against the angiosperm strategy of insect and animal pollination, fruit dispersal and rapid life cycles.

items: Seeds and pollen remove the dependence on free water for fertilisation, which is the advance of the seed plants.
Gymnosperms: naked seeds on cone scales; conifers, cycads and Ginkgo; usually evergreen with needle leaves.
Angiosperms: seed enclosed in a fruit, flowers as reproductive organs, double fertilisation and triploid endosperm.
Double fertilisation gives embryo and endosperm together, so nutrition is supplied only after successful fertilisation.
Angiosperm xylem contains vessel elements; gymnosperm xylem generally has tracheids only.
Pollination in conifers is by wind, while angiosperms use insects, birds, bats and wind with showy or scented flowers.
The fruit protects the seed and aids dispersal by wind, water, animals or explosive mechanisms.

items.note: The scales of a female cone carry two ovules each, and after pollination by wind-borne pollen the seeds develop between the scales, finally winged for dispersal.
If a flower is not pollinated, the endosperm does not form, so the plant wastes no food on an ovule that will never develop.

items.meaning: A seed plant whose seeds are borne naked on cone scales rather than inside a fruit.
A flowering plant with seeds enclosed in a fruit and double fertilisation.
The fusion of one sperm with the egg and a second with the two polar nuclei.
Nutritive tissue formed after fertilisation that feeds the developing embryo.

blocks.text: Alternation of generations is the pattern that runs through the whole plant kingdom, and it repays careful statement because marks are lost through loose wording. Every plant life cycle alternates between two multicellular phases: a diploid sporophyte, which produces spores by meiosis inside a sporangium, and a haploid gametophyte, which produces gametes by mitosis in an antheridium or archegonium. The fusion of gametes restores the diploid condition as the zygote, and the cycle therefore turns twice through a change of chromosome number: meiosis halves it and fertilisation doubles it. What changes between groups is which generation is dominant and how dependent each phase is on the other. In algae the gametophyte is often dominant or the two are equal, as in the isomorphic brown and red algae. In bryophytes the green leafy plant is the gametophyte and the sporophyte is a small dependent capsule. In pteridophytes the dominant generation reverses: the fern is the sporophyte and the prothallus is a reduced gametophyte. In gymnosperms and angiosperms the sporophyte is overwhelmingly dominant and the gametophyte is reduced to a few cells — the pollen grain and the embryo sac — entirely dependent on the sporophyte, which is why a flowering plant looks the way it does. The evolutionary trend to state in an answer is therefore a progressive reduction of the gametophyte and an increasing dependence of reproduction on the seed rather than on water.

items: Two multicellular phases: diploid sporophyte making spores by meiosis, haploid gametophyte making gametes by mitosis.
Meiosis halves the chromosome number; fertilisation doubles it, so the cycle turns through both changes.
Algae: gametophyte dominant or the two generations isomorphic.
Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant, sporophyte dependent on it for nutrition.
Pteridophytes: sporophyte dominant, gametophyte reduced to the independent prothallus.
Seed plants: sporophyte dominant and the gametophyte reduced to pollen and embryo sac, dependent on the parent.
The trend across the kingdom is a shrinking gametophyte and reproduction increasingly protected within a seed.

blocks.caption: Dominance across the plant groups
rows: reduced to pollen and embryo sac

items.note: The green cushion is the gametophyte and the stalks rising from it with capsules are the sporophytes, still attached and fed by the parent plant.
The tall frond is the sporophyte, and the heart-shaped prothallus that grows from its spore is the gametophyte that produces the next sporophyte.

learn.title: Identifying a plant from a description

blocks.text: Identification questions give a description and ask for the group, and the answer is fastest when the characters are taken in a fixed order. Ask first whether there are vascular tissues and true organs: without them the plant is an alga or a bryophyte, and the presence of a leafy shoot on damp soil with rhizoids rather than roots points to a moss. Ask second whether the plant bears seeds, since seeds divide the seed plants from everything before them, and then whether the seed is enclosed in a fruit, which separates gymnosperms from angiosperms. Ask third what the photosynthetic pigment pattern and stored food are, which is how an algal specimen is assigned to green, brown or red. The habit of adding evidence turns a correct answer into a full-marks answer: quote vascular tissue for a fern, flagellated sperm for a liverwort, a cone for a conifer and double fertilisation for a flowering plant. Two further habits prevent slips. Do not identify a plant from size alone, since a large thallose liverwort may be mistaken for a fern without checking for vascular strands, and always give the character before the group name — the reasoning is the mark.

items: Take the characters in order: vascular tissue, then seed, then enclosure of the seed in a fruit.
No vascular tissue means alga or bryophyte; leafy with rhizoids on damp soil means moss.
Vascular tissue with spores in sori and a heart-shaped prothallus means a fern.
Seed present but naked on cone scales means gymnosperm; seed inside a fruit means angiosperm.
Algal class follows pigments and stored food: starch, laminarin or floridean starch.
Always give the diagnostic character alongside the group name, because the character carries the marks.

items.text: A plant with needle leaves and cones
items.note: Vascular tissue, cones and naked seeds identify a conifer, and the needle leaves with a thick cuticle suggest adaptation to cold or dry conditions.

items.text: A thallus on wet rock with no vascular strands
items.note: No vascular tissue and a thalloid body mean an alga, and green colour with starch storage places it in Chlorophyceae.

keyPoints: The plant kingdom divides into algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
Algae are thalloid with no vascular tissue and are anchored by a holdfast.
Green algae store starch and contain chlorophyll a and b; brown algae store laminarin and contain fucoxanthin; red algae store floridean starch and contain phycoerythrin.
Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant kingdom because their swimming sperm need water.
In bryophytes the gametophyte is dominant and the sporophyte is dependent on it.
Pteridophytes were the first vascular plants, with true roots, stems and leaves.
In pteridophytes the sporophyte is dominant and the gametophyte is a small prothallus.
Gymnosperms bear naked seeds on cone scales and have no flowers or fruits.
Angiosperms enclose the seed in a fruit and carry out double fertilisation to form endosperm.
Alternation of generations links a diploid sporophyte making spores by meiosis to a haploid gametophyte making gametes by mitosis.
Across the kingdom the gametophyte becomes progressively reduced while the sporophyte becomes dominant.
The evolution of pollen and then the seed removed the dependence of fertilisation on free water.
examFocus: Comparison tables are the standard form: name the feature in the left column and one entry per group.
Life-cycle questions must name the dominant generation for each group before describing the stages.
Algae questions are marked on pigment, stored food and wall composition — quote all three.
Identification answers must give the diagnostic character before the group name.

vocabulary.meaning: A plant body undifferentiated into root, stem and leaf.
The diploid generation that produces spores by meiosis.
The haploid generation that produces gametes by mitosis.
The small heart-shaped gametophyte of a fern.
A cluster of sporangia on the underside of a fern frond.
A seed plant with naked seeds borne on cone scales.
A flowering plant with seeds in a fruit and double fertilisation.
Triploid nutritive tissue formed after double fertilisation.

questions.prompt: The group of plants that shows double fertilisation is:
questions.explanation: Double fertilisation, giving embryo and triploid endosperm, is peculiar to the flowering plants.

questions.prompt: Which stored food characterises the brown algae?
questions.explanation: Phaeophyceae store laminarin and mannitol, while green algae store starch and red algae floridean starch.

questions.prompt: In bryophytes the dominant generation is the:
questions.explanation: The green leafy plant we see is the gametophyte, and the sporophyte remains attached and dependent on it.

questions.prompt: Which feature first appears in the pteridophytes?
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes are the first plants with xylem and phloem, which is why they can grow upright and larger.

questions.prompt: The body of an alga that is not differentiated into root, stem and leaf is called a __________.
questions.explanation: The thalloid habit is why algae were once grouped as Thallophyta.

questions.prompt: In ferns the small heart-shaped gametophyte that grows from a spore is called the __________.
questions.explanation: It lives independently on damp soil and produces the flagellated sperm.

questions.prompt: Compare the green algae and the red algae with respect to pigments, stored food and reproduction.
questions.answer: Green algae contain chlorophyll a and b with carotenoids, the same pigments as higher plants, and they store food as starch in pyrenoids. Red algae contain chlorophyll a and d together with the red pigment phycoerythrin, which absorbs the blue light that penetrates deepest into the sea, and they store floridean starch. In reproduction the green algae produce flagellated male gametes in many genera, whereas red algae have no flagellated cells at all: the male gamete, or spermatangium, is non-motile and is carried to the carpogonium by water currents.
questions.explanation: Three points of comparison: pigments, stored food and the presence or absence of flagellated gametes.

questions.prompt: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
questions.answer: Bryophytes live on damp soil and are photosynthetic, which is a terrestrial habit, yet their antherozoids are flagellated and must swim through a film of water to reach the egg in the archegonium. Their fertilisation therefore still depends on external water just as an amphibian’s does, and their spores are released only when conditions are moist. They are consequently restricted to damp, shaded habitats despite being land plants.
questions.explanation: Photosynthetic on land but dependent on water for the swimming sperm, with the habitat consequence.

questions.prompt: State two differences between a gymnosperm and an angiosperm.
questions.answer: Gymnosperms bear their seeds naked on the scales of a cone, whereas angiosperms enclose the seed within a fruit that develops from the ovary. Gymnosperms have cones as their reproductive structures and lack double fertilisation, while angiosperms have flowers and undergo double fertilisation to form the triploid endosperm. Their xylem also differs, since angiosperms possess vessel elements and most gymnosperms have tracheids only.
questions.explanation: Any two of naked against enclosed seeds, cone against flower, double fertilisation, or vessels against tracheids.

questions.prompt: Explain alternation of generations and describe how it differs between bryophytes, pteridophytes and angiosperms.
questions.answer: Alternation of generations is the regular alternation between two multicellular phases in the plant life cycle. The diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis within a sporangium; each spore germinates by mitosis into a haploid gametophyte, which produces gametes also by mitosis in antheridia or archegonia; the fusion of gametes restores the diploid zygote, which develops into a new sporophyte. The chromosome number therefore halves at meiosis and is restored at fertilisation. In bryophytes the gametophyte is the dominant phase: the green leafy or thalloid plant is the gametophyte, and the sporophyte is a small capsule of seta and sporangium that remains attached to and nutritionally dependent on it. In pteridophytes the dominance reverses, since the fern is a large vascular sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves, while the gametophyte is reduced to a small heart-shaped prothallus that lives independently on damp soil but still needs water for its swimming sperm. In angiosperms the sporophyte is overwhelmingly dominant and the gametophyte is reduced to a few cells contained within the flower — the pollen grain as the male gametophyte and the embryo sac as the female — entirely dependent on the parent sporophyte, and fertilisation is achieved through pollen tubes without any need for external water.
questions.explanation: The general cycle with both ploidy changes, then the dominant generation and the size and dependence of each phase in the three groups.

questions.prompt: A plant is described as having a flat green thallus on damp soil, no vascular tissue, rhizoids rather than roots, and a dependent capsule on a stalk arising from its upper surface. Identify the group and generation of the plant and justify each feature.
questions.answer: The absence of vascular tissue excludes pteridophytes and seed plants, since no xylem or phloem is present, and the plant must therefore be an alga or a bryophyte. Rhizoids that anchor rather than absorb, together with a differentiated leafy or thalloid body on damp soil, indicate a bryophyte rather than an alga, which would be a simpler thallus usually in water. The flat green body is the gametophyte, the haploid dominant generation that photosynthesises and produces gametes in antheridia and archegonia; the flagellated sperm need a film of water, which the damp habitat supplies. The dependent capsule on a stalk is the sporophyte, consisting of foot, seta and capsule, which remains attached to the gametophyte and draws nutrition from it — the defining condition of bryophytes. The capsule releases spores formed by meiosis, which germinate into new gametophytes. Every feature therefore agrees: a bryophyte, photographed in its gametophyte generation with the sporophyte still attached.
questions.explanation: Each observation addressed: no vascular tissue excludes higher groups, rhizoids indicate bryophyte, the green body is the gametophyte and the capsule the dependent sporophyte.

questions.prompt: Explain how the seed and the pollen grain freed plants from their dependence on water, and give one advantage each of that freedom for gymnosperms and angiosperms.
questions.answer: In algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes the male gamete is flagellated and must swim to the egg, so fertilisation can occur only in a film of water and reproduction is confined to damp habitats. Seed plants evolved the pollen grain, which is the male gametophyte reduced to a few cells protected by a tough wall: it is carried by wind or animals to the ovule, where it germinates into a pollen tube that delivers non-flagellated sperm directly to the egg. The seed then protects the embryo with a coat, holds a supply of food in the endosperm or cotyledons, and can remain dormant until conditions suit germination. For gymnosperms the advantage is that cones and wind-borne pollen allow reproduction in cold and dry habitats where no standing water exists, which is why conifers dominate boreal forests. For angiosperms the advantage is greater still: enclosure of the seed in a fruit allows dispersal by animals, water and wind, and the flower permits precise pollination relationships with insects and birds, together with a rapid life cycle that has made flowering plants the dominant vegetation on land.
questions.explanation: The mechanism of pollen and seed, then one specific advantage for each group tied to its habitat or strategy.
